:::{#exm-uniform-not-exponential-family}
#### The uniform distribution on ${[0, \highend]}$ is not an exponential family

<!-- no-figure: the example compares two density values at one point -->

Let $\Rvar \sim \operatorname{Uniform}(0, \highend)$,
the [uniform distribution](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-uniform) on the [interval](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mcs/sets.html#def-interval) from $0$ to $\highend > 0$.
Its [density](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/random-variables.html#def-pdf) is

$$
\pdf\paren{\rvar ; \highend}
= \begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{\highend}, & 0 \le \rvar \le \highend \\
0, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
$$

Suppose these densities were those of an [exponential family](#def-exponential-family),
indexed by some parameter $\natparam$ that determines $\highend$.
Then @eq-exponential-family would give

$$
\pdf\paren{\rvar ; \natparam}
= \basemeasuref{\rvar} \, \expf{\natparam \, \statf{\rvar} - \logpartitionf{\natparam}}.
$$

The [exponential function](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mds/algebra-exponentials.html#def-exponential-function) is positive
for every $\natparam$ and every $\rvar$,
so $\pdf\paren{\rvar ; \natparam} > 0$
exactly when $\basemeasuref{\rvar} > 0$.
The set of values $\rvar$ with a positive density would then be the same for every parameter value.

The uniform density does depend on it.
At $\rvar = 3/2$, the density is $1/2$
when $\highend = 2$
and $0$
when $\highend = 1$.
So the uniform densities on $[0, \highend]$ are not an exponential family.
The set of values $\rvar$ with a positive density depends on the parameter,
which the form of @eq-exponential-family does not allow.
:::
